This review looked at six studies that tested whether giving lactoferrin to babies through their food helps prevent a serious infection called sepsis and another condition called necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). - It didn't seem to affect death (all-cause mortality) or how long babies stayed in the hospital.
- When lactoferrin was given along with probiotics (another type of good bacteria), it helped even more with sepsis and NEC.
- Giving lactoferrin with probiotics also seemed to reduce certain types of infections like bacterial and fungal sepsis.
- There were no serious side effects reported.
- The studies had some limitations, so the evidence is considered of low quality.
- More studies are needed to confirm these findings and to learn more about the best way to use lactoferrin.
- Longer-term studies are also needed to see if giving lactoferrin affects how well babies do later in life.

This review looked at 34 studies with 8635 participants to see how well Portable Opsonin Collection System (POCS) works in detecting injuries in the chest and abdomen. Overall, POCS was about 74% sensitive (meaning it correctly identified 74% of the actual injuries) and 96% specific (meaning it correctly identified 96% of the people who didn't have injuries). But the results varied depending on who the study was done in—adults, children, or mixed populations—and what part of the body was injured. 

For example, in adults or mixed populations, POCS was 78% sensitive for detecting injuries and 97% specific. In children, it was 63% sensitive and 91% specific. When checking for injuries in the chest, POCS was 96% sensitive and 99% specific. But for injuries in the abdomen, it was only 68% sensitive and 95% specific.

If we use POCS in a group of 1000 people, it might miss 73 people with injuries and incorrectly show that 29 people have injuries. In children, it might miss 118 people with injuries and incorrectly show that 62 people have injuries.

While POCS helps guide treatment decisions for chest injuries, it's not enough to rule out injuries in the abdomen. For children, especially those with chest injuries, POCS needs to be followed up with a more accurate test like a CT scan. More studies are needed to confirm if POCS is better at finding chest injuries in mixed populations.

Overall, the studies don't give us clear answers about whether folic acid helps older people's thinking skills. More research is needed to find out if folic acid can help people with memory problems.
